Ezra 1.audience: The first readers were the returned exiles and their children. This chapter opens with Cyrus' decree in his first year as ruler of Babylon, 538 BC.

culture.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
culture.text: A clay cylinder of Cyrus, found in Babylon, describes him returning peoples to their lands and restoring the shrines of their gods—the same policy as his decree for the Jews.

culture.title: Returning the temple vessels
culture.text: Cyrus returns 5,400 gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods.

Ezra 2.audience: This register lists the families who returned, by clan and by town. Readers could find their own families in it; the same list appears in Nehemiah 7.

culture.title: Priests without records
culture.text: Some priests could not find their family registry and were barred from the priesthood until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim.

culture.title: Servants and singers
culture.text: The whole company numbered 42,360, plus 7,337 servants and 200 singing men and women.

culture.title: Gifts by weight
culture.text: Families gave 61,000 drams (darics) of gold and 5,000 pounds (minas) of silver for the work, along with priests' garments.

Ezra 3.audience: The altar is rebuilt and the temple foundation laid. Readers would remember the mixed sounds of shouting for joy and the weeping of old men who had seen the first temple (Ezra 3:12).

culture.title: The altar before the temple
culture.text: Sacrifices resume on the rebuilt altar even before the temple foundation is laid, on the old site, "for fear was upon them because of the people of those countries."

culture.title: Cedar by sea to Joppa
culture.text: As in Solomon's day, cedar is brought from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, paid for with food, drink, and oil.

Ezra 4.audience: Opposition from neighboring peoples stops the work. This chapter gathers examples of opposition from several Persian reigns, not all in order.

culture.title: Letters in Aramaic
culture.text: From Ezra 4:8 to 6:18 the text is in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, quoting letters to and from the king.

culture.title: Royal archives
culture.text: The enemies ask the king to search "the book of the records of thy fathers." Persian kings kept archives of past decrees and events.

culture.title: Peoples resettled by Assyria
culture.text: The adversaries say they have worshipped Israel's God since Esarhaddon king of Assyria brought them to the land.

Ezra 5.audience: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir the people to resume building (Ezra 5:1). Readers knew their messages from the books named after them.

culture.title: Tatnai the governor
culture.text: Tatnai was governor "on this side the river"—the Persian province west of the Euphrates. A Babylonian tablet names a governor Tattenai of this province.

culture.title: Great stones and timber
culture.text: The temple was built "with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls"—courses of wood set between layers of stone, a common building method.

Ezra 6.audience: Cyrus' decree is found in the royal archives, and the temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Readers worshipped in this second temple.

culture.title: Achmetha
culture.text: The scroll is found at Achmetha (Ecbatana), the summer capital of the Persian kings in Media.

culture.title: Impaling for disobedience
culture.text: Darius decrees that anyone who changes his order is to be hanged (impaled) on a beam from his own house. Persian kings used such severe punishments.

culture.title: The month Adar
culture.text: Adar was the twelfth month, in February–March. The temple was finished just before the new year.

Ezra 7.audience: Ezra arrives in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, about 458 BC, nearly sixty years after the temple was finished. Readers knew him as "a ready scribe in the law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6).

culture.title: A royal letter of authority
culture.text: Artaxerxes' letter in Aramaic gives Ezra authority to teach the law, appoint judges, and draw on the royal treasury. Persian kings gave local peoples authority to keep their own laws.

culture.title: A four-month journey
culture.text: Ezra leaves Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrives in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month.

Ezra 8.audience: Ezra lists the families who traveled with him and the treasure they carried. Readers would see him refuse an armed escort, trusting God for protection (Ezra 8:22).

culture.title: Weighing the treasure
culture.text: Ezra weighs out silver, gold, and vessels to the priests before the journey, and they are weighed again in the temple on arrival (Ezra 8:33–34).

culture.title: Fasting by the river
culture.text: Ezra proclaims a fast at the river Ahava before setting out, to seek "a right way" for the travelers and their goods.

Ezra 9.audience: Ezra learns that people, priests, and Levites have married foreign wives. Readers would hear his prayer of confession for the whole community.

culture.title: Pulling out hair
culture.text: Ezra tears his clothes and plucks out hair from his head and beard—extreme signs of grief and shock.

culture.title: The evening sacrifice
culture.text: Ezra prays "at the evening sacrifice," the regular afternoon offering at the temple.

Ezra 10.audience: The people gather in the rain to deal with the mixed marriages, and the book ends with a list of the men involved. Readers would recognize the families named.

culture.title: Assembly in the rain
culture.text: The assembly meets in the ninth month (December), in the cold rainy season, and the people sit in the street "trembling because of this matter, and for the great rain."

culture.title: Forfeiting property
culture.text: Anyone who did not come within three days would forfeit his property and be separated from the congregation.

Nehemiah 1.audience: Nehemiah writes in his own voice. He was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes at Shushan (Susa), the Persian winter capital, in 445 BC.

culture.title: Shushan the palace
culture.text: Shushan (Susa) was a royal capital of Persia. Excavations have uncovered the palace of Darius there.

culture.title: Burned gates
culture.text: City gates were made of wood set in stone gateways. Jerusalem's had been burned, leaving the city open to attack.

Nehemiah 2.audience: Nehemiah receives the king's permission and letters to rebuild Jerusalem's walls. Readers would see opposition begin at once from Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem.

culture.title: The cupbearer
culture.text: A cupbearer tasted and served the king's wine and was a trusted courtier with direct access to the king.

culture.title: A sad face before the king
culture.text: Servants were expected to show a cheerful face in the king's presence. Nehemiah is "very sore afraid" when the king notices his sadness.

culture.title: Sanballat and Geshem
culture.text: An Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine in Egypt names Sanballat as governor of Samaria, and an inscription names a Geshem king of Kedar.

Nehemiah 3.audience: Families, priests, goldsmiths, merchants, and town leaders each repair a section of the wall, often near their own homes. Readers would find their families' work recorded.

culture.title: Jerusalem's gates
culture.text: The gates are listed in order around the city—the sheep gate, fish gate, old gate, valley gate, dung gate, fountain gate, water gate, horse gate, and others—tracing the wall's circuit.

culture.title: Nobles who would not work
culture.text: The nobles of Tekoa "put not their necks to the work," an image from oxen refusing the yoke.

Nehemiah 4.audience: The builders face mockery and threats of attack. Readers would see them work with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4:17).

culture.title: Rubbish and burned stones
culture.text: Sanballat mocks the builders for trying to revive "the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned"—limestone damaged by fire crumbles.

culture.title: A trumpet to gather
culture.text: A trumpeter stays beside Nehemiah so that workers spread along the wall can be gathered quickly if attacked.

Nehemiah 5.audience: Poor Jews have mortgaged fields and sold children to pay debts and Persian taxes. Readers would see Nehemiah stop the practice and give up his own governor's allowance.

culture.title: Debt and the king's tribute
culture.text: Families borrowed money to pay the king's tax, pledging their fields and vineyards. Persian taxes were collected in silver.

culture.title: Shaking out the lap
culture.text: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a sign of how God would shake out anyone who broke the promise.

culture.title: The governor's bread
culture.text: Earlier governors took food, wine, and forty shekels of silver from the people. Nehemiah refused the governor's allowance.

Nehemiah 6.audience: The wall is finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). Readers would see Nehemiah resist plots to lure him out or frighten him into the temple.

culture.title: An open letter
culture.text: Sanballat sends his servant with "an open letter in his hand." Official letters were sealed; an open letter could be read by anyone, spreading the rumor.

culture.title: Hiding in the temple
culture.text: Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple. As a layman, Nehemiah would not enter the holy place.

Nehemiah 7.audience: Jerusalem has walls but few inhabitants (Nehemiah 7:4). Nehemiah finds the register of the first returnees, repeated here from Ezra 2.

culture.title: Gates opened in daylight
culture.text: The gates were not to be opened "until the sun be hot" and were shut and barred while the watchmen stood guard.

culture.title: Gifts to the work
culture.text: The governor, the chief fathers, and the people give gold drams, silver pounds, basins, and priests' garments.

Nehemiah 8.audience: Ezra reads the law aloud to men, women, and children who could understand, from morning until midday (Nehemiah 8:2–3). Readers would see the community hear and respond to the law.

culture.title: A wooden pulpit
culture.text: Ezra stands on a raised wooden platform so the crowd can see and hear him.

culture.title: Giving the sense
culture.text: Levites read "distinctly, and gave the sense" so the people understood. Many returnees spoke Aramaic and needed the Hebrew text explained.

culture.title: Booths on roofs
culture.text: The people build booths on their roofs, in their courtyards, in the temple courts, and in the streets for the feast of tabernacles.

Nehemiah 9.audience: The Levites lead a long prayer that retells Israel's history from creation to the exile. Readers would hear their own story confessed as they lived under foreign rule: "we are servants this day" (Nehemiah 9:36).

culture.title: Sackcloth and earth
culture.text: The people fast in sackcloth with earth on their heads—signs of mourning and repentance.

culture.title: Standing for the reading
culture.text: The people stand while the law is read for a quarter of the day and confess for another quarter.

Nehemiah 10.audience: Leaders, Levites, and priests seal a written covenant. Readers would see the community commit to specific obligations: no mixed marriages, keeping the Sabbath, and supporting the temple.

culture.title: Sealing a document
culture.text: Documents were sealed with clay impressions of personal seals. Hundreds of such seal impressions (bullae) have been found in Judah.

culture.title: A third of a shekel
culture.text: The people pledge a third of a shekel each year for the temple service. In later times the yearly temple tax was a half-shekel (Matthew 17:24).

culture.title: The wood offering
culture.text: Families take turns, by lot, bringing wood for the altar fire at set times each year.

Nehemiah 11.audience: One in ten of the people is chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1). Readers would see the city repopulated with families from Judah and Benjamin.

culture.title: Volunteers for the city
culture.text: The people bless those who willingly offer to live in Jerusalem. Living in the city meant leaving one's farmland.

culture.title: Villages around
culture.text: Others live in the villages of Judah and Benjamin, from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom.

Nehemiah 12.audience: The priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel are listed, then the dedication of the wall is described. Readers would see two choirs walk the walls in opposite directions and meet at the temple.

culture.title: Processions on the wall
culture.text: The wall was wide enough to walk on. Two great companies of singers walk around it from the valley gate in opposite directions.

culture.title: Joy heard afar off
culture.text: The rejoicing of men, women, and children "was heard even afar off."

Nehemiah 13.audience: Nehemiah returns from a visit to the king and finds the covenant broken—a room in the temple given to Tobiah, Levites unpaid, Sabbath trade, and mixed marriages. The book ends with his reforms and prayer.

culture.title: Sabbath markets
culture.text: Men tread winepresses and bring grain, wine, and figs into Jerusalem on the Sabbath, and Tyrian merchants sell fish. Nehemiah shuts the gates from dusk before the Sabbath.

culture.title: The speech of Ashdod
culture.text: Children of mixed marriages spoke the language of Ashdod and could not speak the Jews' language.

culture.title: Pulling out hair
culture.text: Nehemiah curses and strikes some of the men and pulls out their hair—a public shaming.
